# CasScheme0 — the production hash ruling (H1–H6)

STATUS: G0 decision docket, pending ratification. The estate's models
are deliberately digest-abstract and stay that way; this docket pins
the PRODUCTION address scheme the published package ships, which
nothing can interoperate without.

## H1 — Digest algorithm: SHA-256 (recommended)

Candidates were SHA-256 and BLAKE3. SHA-256 through WebCrypto is
available in every target runtime (browser, Node, Bun, Deno) with
zero new dependencies, hardware acceleration, and three decades of
scrutiny; the package keeps its single-dependency posture. BLAKE3 is
faster and carries the bao heritage, but it is absent from WebCrypto,
so it would arrive as a WASM or native dependency — new supply-chain
surface and per-platform variance — and its headline extra (the
internal tree mode) is redundant here: this design builds its OWN
tree over node addresses, so the leaf hash needs to be nothing more
than a boring, universal digest. BLAKE3 remains a natural future
scheme if a native-speed profile ever wants it.

## H2 — Address derivation: the digest of the canonical encoding

`addr(node) = SHA-256(encodeNode(node))`, all thirty-two bytes, never
truncated (the standing full-width ruling). NOTHING is prepended: the
canonical encoding already carries the version byte, kind tag, and
length frames, so domain separation lives inside the digest input —
the same property the model's collision-transfer theorems lean on.
The digest input is EXACTLY the canonical bytes; there is no
secondary serialization to drift (the Unison lesson, taken as a
warning rather than a design).

## H3 — Scheme identity: profile-pinned, no per-address prefix

`cas-http/0` pins scheme 0 globally. Addresses on the wire are the
raw thirty-two bytes (lowercase hex in paths); no multihash-style
per-address prefix — per-address agility buys nothing at one scheme
and costs bytes and parser surface everywhere. Migration to a future
scheme goes through the reserved plane the prior-art review adopted:
a new profile revision, registered decoders per scheme, derived
alias indexes that are never identity evidence, unknown schemes
failing closed.

## H4 — The hash is an injected Effect service

WebCrypto's digest is asynchronous, so the production address
function is Effect-ful. This matches the standing posture (the model
never instantiates the hash; the concrete digest is an injected
adapter): a `CasHash` service with the WebCrypto SHA-256 layer as the
shipped default, the synchronous test digest remaining for fixtures.
Store, transfer, and blob construction already run inside Effect, so
the seam moves no public types — but it is the one API-shaping
consequence of the ruling and the reason the ruling precedes further
client code.

## H5 — Evidence: known-answer fixtures, generated

The committed conformance vectors stay digest-abstract under the
declared toy oracle — that is their design. CasScheme0 gets its own
evidence lane: known-answer fixtures (canonical node bytes → expected
address) GENERATED by a script and committed, per the
generated-vectors law, plus the existing put–get–put round-trip
fixtures running under the production layer. Cross-runtime agreement
(Node, Bun, browser WebCrypto) is asserted by running the same
fixtures in CI's existing matrix.

## H6 — Digests are not secrets

Content addresses need no constant-time comparison; they are public
identity. Constant-time discipline applies to CREDENTIALS, which the
profile's authentication clause owns. What digest exposure does
implicate is the presence-oracle policy the review flagged —
cross-tenant existence probing — and that stays a server policy
concern, not a hash-scheme concern.

## On ratification

The profile gains a "scheme 0" clause; a small implementation packet
lands the `CasHash` service, the WebCrypto layer, and the
known-answer fixtures; the README's claim language names the scheme.
Until then the package cannot interoperate across processes and MUST
NOT publish.
